CONFIRMED, gap is real and current.

CONFIRMED.

6. **NEW, material: "MCP: stdio transport. No network listener" (Security Boundaries, Network Boundary bullet, ~line 518) is STALE.** `cmd/beadle-email/admin_cmd.go:99-121` adds `--transport ws`, which calls `internal/mcp/ws.go`'s `WSServer.ListenAndServe` — a real `net/http` listener on port 8420 (default) serving `/mcp` over WebSocket. `CheckOrigin` unconditionally returns `true` (`ws.go:43`), and **there is no authentication check anywhere in this codebase for the ws transport** — `grep -rn MCP_PROXY_TOKEN --include='*.go' .` returns exactly one hit, a comment saying an *external* `mcp-proxy` component handles auth on upgrade. As shipped in this repo, an unauthenticated network listener exists as an opt-in mode. Proposed replacement:
   > `\item \textbf{MCP}: stdio transport by default; \texttt{--transport ws} opens an HTTP/WebSocket listener (default port 8420) with \texttt{CheckOrigin} accepting all origins and no authentication in this binary --- callers rely on network isolation or an external \texttt{mcp-proxy} enforcing \texttt{MCP\_PROXY\_TOKEN}, which is not verified here.}`

Audit of `docs/architecture.tex` lines 343-435 (Message Send Path, PGP Subsystem). Findings below, numbered. No edits made.

1. **Line 372, `\subsection{PGP Signing (Future)}` + body (374-377) — WRONG.** Outbound signing shipped (DES-022, SETTLED, beadle-atz, PR #132, 2026-04-11; `internal/pgp/sign.go`, `internal/email/send.go`'s `ComposeSignedRaw`/`ComposeEncryptedSignedRaw`, wired in `internal/email/chain.go`'s `TrySendChain`). The claimed remedy is also wrong on the facts: doc says "Amazon SES will be added ... in a future release," but DES-005/DES-006 record SES was never adopted (Resend's own backend *is* SES and still strips `multipart/signed`) — the actual shipped transport is **Fastmail SMTP** (port 465, implicit TLS), operator-configured via `email.json`, verified 2026-04-11 (green GPG Mail checkmark). Proposed replacement:

```latex
\subsection{PGP Signing}

PGP signing of outbound mail is opt-in, controlled by \texttt{gpg\_signer}
in \texttt{email.json} (DES-022, SETTLED, beadle-atz, PR~\#132).  When set,
every outbound message is signed (\texttt{multipart/signed}, RFC~3156);
when empty (the default), mail is sent unsigned.  Signing requires a
MIME-preserving SMTP transport: Proton Bridge strips \texttt{multipart/
signed} envelopes (DES-005), so does Resend/SES (DES-006).  \textbf{Fastmail
SMTP} (port 465, implicit TLS) is the verified MIME-preserving transport
(2026-04-11) --- an operator switches \texttt{email.json} to it to get a
signature that actually verifies on the recipient side.  \texttt{TrySendChain}
does not itself select or validate the transport for MIME preservation; it
sends over whatever SMTP host is configured and reports success on a clean
SMTP transaction, so a signed message sent through the default (Proton
Bridge) config will report \texttt{"sent"} while carrying a broken/stripped
signature on the wire.  When SMTP fails and signing is configured, the
Resend fallback is refused outright (\S\ref{sec:resend-api} below) and the
SMTP error is returned directly --- no silent downgrade to unsigned
delivery.  Encryption (\texttt{ComposeEncryptedSignedRaw}, multipart/
encrypted, RFC~3156) always implies signing; there is no encrypt-without-
sign path, and \texttt{TrySendChain} rejects the combination if
\texttt{recipientKeyIDs} is set without \texttt{gpg\_signer}.
```

2. **Lines 346-357 (`SendState` schema + prose) — STALE.** The schema and its two-branch prose (SMTP-or-Resend) predate signing/encryption entirely and don't model `TrySendChain`'s real branching (3-way compose: plain/signed/encrypted; Resend refusal when signing; implicit-TLS on :465 vs. STARTTLS). Evidence: `internal/email/chain.go:41-145`. Proposed replacement:

```latex
\begin{schema}{SendState}
  smtpAvailable : ZBOOL \\
  signing : ZBOOL \\
  encrypting : ZBOOL \\
  method! : SendMethod
  \where
  encrypting = ztrue \implies signing = ztrue \\
  smtpAvailable = ztrue \implies method! = smSMTP \\
  smtpAvailable = zfalse \land signing = zfalse \implies method! = smResend \\
  smtpAvailable = zfalse \land signing = ztrue \implies method! = smFailed
\end{schema}

The send path attempts the configured SMTP transport first --- Proton
Bridge by default, or another MIME-preserving host (Fastmail) when
signing is configured.  If SMTP is unreachable (a TCP dial to the SMTP
port times out in 2~seconds) \emph{and} signing/encryption is not
configured, the Resend API is used as fallback.  If SMTP fails while
signing or encryption is configured, the Resend fallback is refused and
the SMTP error returned to the caller --- Resend cannot preserve raw MIME
(\S\ref{sec:resend-api}), so falling back would silently ship an unsigned
message under a signed-looking config.
```

3. **Lines 358-364 (`\subsection{Proton Bridge SMTP}`) — STALE, incomplete.** Doc states only STARTTLS with the loopback cert exception. `internal/email/smtp.go:34-63` also implements **implicit TLS on port 465** (PR #133, "implicit TLS for IMAP (993) and SMTP (465)"), which is exactly the branch used for the Fastmail signing transport — omitting it leaves the signing story (finding 1) undocumentable. Proposed addition after line 364: "On port 465, `SMTPSend` dials implicit TLS (SMTPS) directly rather than STARTTLS; this is the branch used for a MIME-preserving transport such as Fastmail." Authentication-via-PLAIN-with-IMAP-fallback-credentials claim (line 361-362) is ACCURATE — confirmed against `SMTPEffectiveUser`/`SMTPEffectivePassword` fallback in `internal/email/config.go`.

4. **Lines 366-370 (`\subsection{Resend API}`) — ACCURATE, not vestigial.** `Send()` in `internal/email/send.go:439` is live, called from `chain.go` as the unsigned-only fallback. One incompleteness: doesn't state the signing-blocks-fallback rule (now covered by findings 1/2's replacement text).

5. **Lines 420-433 (`\subsection{Sign Flow}`) — MISSING a step.** The enumerate has no step for the DES-020 key-expiry rejection. `internal/pgp/sign.go`'s `Sign()` calls `checkSignerKeyExpiry` (wrapping `CheckKeyExpiry`) *before* boundary generation or body composition — it's the first thing that can fail after the CR/LF header check. Propose inserting as new step 1 (renumbering the rest):

```latex
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Reject the signing key if it has no expiration date, or its
    expiration has already passed (DES-020, \texttt{CheckKeyExpiry} via
    \texttt{checkSignerKeyExpiry}).  Applies to the primary key and, if
    the key has signing-capable subkeys, requires at least one currently
    unexpired one.
  \item Compose the body as a MIME part with CRLF line endings
    (mandatory per RFC~3156).
  \item Write the GPG passphrase to a temporary file (mode 600) to
    avoid exposing it in process arguments or \texttt{ps} output.
  \item Run \texttt{gpg --detach-sign --armor} with
    \texttt{--pinentry-mode loopback --passphrase-file} and
    \texttt{-u} set to the signer.
  \item Assemble the full RFC~822 message with a
    \texttt{multipart/signed} envelope containing the body part and
    detached signature.
  \item Generate the MIME boundary using \texttt{crypto/rand}.
\end{enumerate}
```

6. **Sign vs. verify keyring asymmetry (lines 397-399, 420-433) — ACCURATE, confirm both halves.** Verify (`internal/pgp/verify.go:42-51`) always runs in a fresh `/tmp/bg-*` GNUPGHOME. Sign (`internal/pgp/sign.go`'s `detachSign`) and Decrypt (`internal/pgp/decrypt.go:30`, doc comment "unlike Verify, Decrypt uses the default GNUPGHOME because the agent's private key lives in the system keyring") both use the ambient/system keyring directly, no isolation. Doc's Design Invariants section (line 478-482, out of my assigned range) already states the rationale correctly; the PGP Subsystem section itself doesn't restate it, which is fine — no fix needed here, just confirming it isn't contradicted.

7. **Second verification path entirely absent — MISSING, the largest finding in my range.** `internal/daemon/signature.go`'s `VerifySignature` (DES-034 SETTLED beadle-iru; wired via DES-035 SETTLED into `LoadCommands`/`loadCommand` in `internal/daemon/command.go`) is a structurally distinct verification flow from `pgp.Verify` and is not mentioned anywhere in the PGP Subsystem section: canonical-subset signing (`CanonicalCommandBytes` — marshal the command with `Signature` cleared to `""`, so the signature covers exactly the rest of the command file, deterministically, via yaml.v3's stable field/map ordering), single-fingerprint-only isolated keyring (imports *only* the configured authorizer key, then asserts exactly one matching `fpr` record landed — zero or >1 is a hard `SignatureError`, never "verify against whatever's there"), and GnuPG **status-fd** classification (`--status-fd 1`, parsing `[GNUPG:] GOODSIG/EXPKEYSIG/NO_PUBKEY/BADSIG/ERRSIG/REVKEYSIG/EXPSIG` machine-readable lines) rather than `pgp.Verify`'s stderr-substring parsing ("Good signature from"). This is deliberately the stricter of the two: it authorizes daemon command *execution* (zero-agent-authority boundary), where `pgp.Verify` only classifies inbound-message trust level. Propose a new subsection after Sign Flow:

```latex
\subsection{Command-File Signature Verification (DES-034, DES-035)}

A separate, stricter verification path,
\texttt{daemon.VerifySignature(cmd, gpgBinary, ownerKeyID)}, authorizes
\texttt{beadle-daemon} command files before they are loaded
(\texttt{LoadCommands}/\texttt{loadCommand} in
\texttt{internal/daemon/command.go}) --- distinct from
\texttt{pgp.Verify}, which classifies inbound message trust.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Reconstruct the canonical signed bytes:
    \texttt{CanonicalCommandBytes} marshals the command with its
    \texttt{Signature} field cleared, so the signature covers exactly the
    rest of the file, deterministically (yaml.v3's stable field and
    sorted-map ordering).
  \item Create an isolated GNUPGHOME (same \texttt{/tmp/bg-*} pattern as
    \texttt{pgp.Verify}).
  \item Export \emph{only} the configured authorizer key\footnote{Named
    \texttt{owner\_handle}/\texttt{owner\_gpg\_key\_id} in
    \texttt{daemon.json} and code today; a narrower name than "owner"
    implies --- it authorizes recipe/command files only, not a general
    position of authority. Rename tracked as beadle-4ul, not yet done.}
    from the ambient keyring into the isolated one, and assert exactly
    one key with that exact fingerprint landed --- zero or ambiguous
    matches fail closed.
  \item Check that key's expiry (DES-020) against the isolated homedir.
  \item Run \texttt{gpg --status-fd 1 --verify} and classify the
    machine-readable \texttt{[GNUPG:]} status lines: \texttt{GOODSIG} to
    accept; \texttt{NO\_PUBKEY} to \texttt{wrong-key};
    \texttt{EXPKEYSIG} to \texttt{key-expired};
    \texttt{BADSIG}/\texttt{ERRSIG}/\texttt{REVKEYSIG}/\texttt{EXPSIG}
    and any unrecognized outcome to \texttt{invalid}.  Every branch
    except \texttt{GOODSIG} is a non-nil error --- there is no implicit
    fallthrough to success.
\end{enumerate}
```

(Footnote flags the "owner" naming per your instruction — not rewritten elsewhere, since it doesn't otherwise appear in my assigned line range.)

**Not independently re-verified:** the exact wire behavior of Proton Bridge stripping signed envelopes today (relying on DES-005's 2026-03-13 test record, not a fresh repro) and Fastmail's current behavior (relying on DES-022/TESTING.md's 2026-04-11 record). Both are cited, not re-run.

Everything else in the assigned range (`GPGEnvironment` schema lines 388-395, Verify Flow enumerate lines 403-418, PGP Subsystem intro lines 383-386) checked ACCURATE against `internal/pgp/verify.go` and `internal/daemon/signature.go` — no changes proposed.

1. `\section{Daemon Architecture (DES-027/028/029)}` — verdict STALE. DESIGN.md:1641 states DES-028 itself is "Superseded by DES-031" — so the heading already names a superseded ADR as if current, and omits DES-030 through DES-036 entirely. **Recommend dropping DES numbers from the heading** — use `\section{Daemon Architecture}` and cite specific DES-### numbers inline next to the claims they support, the way the rest of the doc does for the trust model. A heading enumerating ADRs will keep going stale; agreed with your instinct.

**§Detection and Trust Gate (lines 553-567)**
2. Steps 1-5 (fetch → contact lookup → x-bit → trust verify → create pipeline) — verdict ACCURATE. Matches `internal/daemon/handler.go:135-224` (`OnNewMail`) exactly, including step order.
3. MISSING: step 5 "creates a pipeline" only happens when `spawner != nil && templates != nil` (i.e. an API key is configured). Without one, `handler.go:216` falls back to `h.missions.Create(meta)` — a bare mission record, no Executor pipeline. 4. TODO markers confirmed present verbatim: `handler.go:160` `// TODO(beadle-xxx): verify IMAP is localhost as additional guard.` and `handler.go:233` same pattern — this is your beadle-hv7i gap. Note the TODO text literally says `beadle-xxx`, not a real bead ID — worth flagging that it's an unfiled placeholder in code, not just an untracked concern.

5. `"[cmd1 | cmd2 | ... | auto-reply] -> Sequential mission execution"` with `inputs.previous_output` — WRONG on two counts: (a) this is the v1 linear model DES-031 replaced (`internal/daemon/pipeline.go:132-172`, `Executor.Run`'s sequential loop over `Runner.Run`, with `process`/`passthrough` mode branching at line 155); (b) the field name is wrong — it's `context`, not `inputs.previous_output` or `inputs.pipeline_output`. Confirmed at `pipeline.go:209-215`'s doc comment: *"ethos's inputs schema recognizes only trigger, files, ticket, and references... there is no inputs.args or inputs.pipeline_output. Stage args and the prior stage's pipeline output are carried instead as free text in the top-level context field"* — this is literally the beadle-8gt regression your brief mentions.
6. MISSING: CLI runner compound `steps` via `io.Pipe` goroutines — confirmed at `internal/daemon/runner.go:302-434` (`runCompound`), each step wired via `io.Pipe()`, run concurrently, waited via `sync.WaitGroup`. Also missing: 1 MB output cap via `io.LimitReader` (`runner.go:230`, `readCapped`, `cappedWriter` type at line 446), binary whitelist with `filepath.EvalSymlinks` re-validation (`runner.go:98-129`, `BinaryWhitelist.Resolve`), and `output_schema` JSON-schema validation on process-mode stages (`pipeline.go:101-114`, `ValidateOutput`/`CompileSchema`).
7. Proposed replacement text (matches doc's existing style):

```latex
A pipeline decomposes an email instruction into a sequence of typed
commands (DES-031).  Each command is a GPG-signed YAML definition
(DES-034/035) with a typed argument schema, write-set, budget,
timeout, and tool list, and runs in one of two modes: \texttt{process}
(its output replaces the pipe) or \texttt{passthrough} (the pipe
carries forward unchanged, for side-effect commands such as
notifications).

\begin{verbatim}
  Email instruction
    -> Planner (rule-based; LLM planner is a stub, DES-tl6)
    -> pipe = email metadata JSON
    -> for each stage: pipe = runner.Run(stage, pipe)  (process mode)
                        runner.Run(stage, pipe)         (passthrough)
    -> auto-appended reply stage with final pipe value
\end{verbatim}

Two runners execute a stage (DES-030): \texttt{claude} spawns an
ephemeral mission via the shared Executor path, and \texttt{cli} runs
a whitelisted binary directly, either singly or as a compound chain of
steps wired stdin/stdout through \texttt{io.Pipe} as concurrent
goroutines --- one pipe value, no accumulator.  CLI output is capped
at 1\,MB via \texttt{io.LimitReader}; a process-mode command's output
is additionally validated against its declared \texttt{output\_schema}
before becoming the next stage's pipe value.  Stage args and the prior
stage's pipe value are carried into the mission contract's top-level
\texttt{context} field --- ethos's contract schema has no
\texttt{inputs.pipeline\_output} field; an earlier design that assumed
one shipped broken (beadle-8gt) until corrected.

\textbf{Designed but not implemented (DES-032, PROPOSED):} attachments
and generated files as a second \texttt{files} array riding alongside
the JSON pipe.  \texttt{Command} carries no file-flow fields today ---
verified against \texttt{internal/daemon/command.go}.
```

**§Auto-Reply (DES-029) (lines 587-596)**
8. Verdict ACCURATE. `pipeline.go:174-202` auto-appends a `reply` stage with the final pipe value after the last planned stage; `fireElse` (`pipeline.go:365-402`) sends a fixed-text error reply on any failure path. "Originator never receives silence" holds — every failure branch in `Executor.Run` calls `e.fireElse(p)`.

**§Worker Isolation (lines 598-610)**
9. `--bare` mode, restricted PATH, per-command MCP registry, adversarial system prompt, 30-min/\$5/50-turn limits, protected env vars forced after overrides — verdict ACCURATE, confirmed line-for-line against `internal/daemon/spawner.go:63-183` and the adversarial-instructions comment in `templates.go:90`. Recommend appending one sentence: *"This is environment- and permission-level isolation, not OS-level sandboxing --- there is no container, network-namespace, or seccomp boundary; TODO in spawner.go, currently unfiled as a bead."*

**§Pipeline Persistence (lines 612-617)**
11. Verdict ACCURATE and now materially true (was previously false, per your brief). Confirmed: `internal/daemon/persist.go` `Save` does atomic write-then-rename (`os.WriteFile` to `.tmp-<id>.json` then `os.Rename`, lines 66-91), path-traversal guard (line 67: rejects `/`, `\`, `..`, empty ID), 0700 dir / 0600 file modes. `cmd/beadle-daemon/main.go:59-72` wires `store := &daemon.PipelineStore{...}` into the handler and calls `store.StartPruning(daemon.DefaultRetention)` — confirmed the `Store` field is now actually populated in `main.go`, not just in tests (I checked; previously it apparently wasn't). `sweepStalePipelines` (`main.go:193-207`) marks in-flight pipelines failed on startup via `LoadRunning`. 30-day retention (`DefaultRetention`, `persist.go:63`) pruned by a recurring ticker (`StartPruning`/`DefaultPruneInterval` = 24h, `persist.go:282-332`), not just at startup — confirmed as a real fix, not just a startup-only sweep.
12. MISSING detail worth adding: orphaned `.tmp-*.json` files (crash between write and rename) are separately reaped after 5 minutes (`tmpFileMaxAge`, `persist.go:147`) — a second, distinct cleanup concern from the 30-day content retention. One clause would suffice.

**Cross-cutting gaps confirmed present in code, not yet in this section at all — all governing-rule "retain and label" cases:**
13. DES-034/035 (signature verification, wired) — real. `internal/daemon/signature.go`'s `VerifySignature`; `command.go:88-159` (`LoadCommands`/`loadCommand`) calls it when `ownerKeyID != ""`. `main.go:121,231-246` (`resolveDaemonOwnerKeyID`): absent/unresolvable/ambiguous `daemon.json` → `loadCommandsEnabled=false` → zero commands loaded, never falls back to unsigned. This section says nothing about signature verification at all today — it's the single largest missing piece besides the v1/v2 pipeline gap.
14. DES-036 (dev/CI-parity test tier, PR #261) — real, not mentioned in this section; arguably belongs in TESTING.md rather than here, no action needed unless you want a cross-reference.
15. beadle-tl6 (LLMPlanner stub) — confirmed, `internal/daemon/planner.go:63-69`, `Plan` returns `fmt.Errorf("LLMPlanner not yet implemented")` unconditionally. Production planner wired in `main.go:134-150` is a `RulePlanner` with exactly one hardcoded rule (`(?i)summarize|summary` → `summarize` command).
16. beadle-ivtd (planner regex untested) — confirmed by absence: `grep -rn "summarize|summary"` across `*_test.go` in `cmd/beadle-daemon/` and `internal/daemon/` returns nothing. The production rule in `main.go` has no test coverage.
17. beadle-hv7i — confirmed via TODO markers cited in #4 above.
18. beadle-623 (no audit log implementation) — confirmed by absence: no file implementing an append-only signed audit log anywhere under `internal/`; the only "audit" hits are ethos's own `internal/enable/enable.go` (unrelated — that's ethos's own audit-seal git hook, not beadle's).
19. beadle-7gm (no init/sign tooling) — not directly in this section's scope, already covered accurately in ARCHITECTURE.md; no action needed here unless you want a one-line pointer.

**"Owner" terminology (beadle-4ul, flagged not rewritten per your instruction):** lines 549-551 ("authorised contacts") and none of my section's other prose use the word "owner" directly — the section is clean on this point as written. (The signature-verification text I'm proposing to add in #7/#13 would need to say "owner key" per current code naming in `daemon.json`'s `owner_handle`/`owner_gpg_key_id` — flagging that the replacement text I drafted, if adopted, will reintroduce "owner" language matching current code, not the renamed term.)

Also did not verify DES-033 (repo tagging/scoping) since it's outside this section's line range, though `main.go:158-160` shows the daemon poller explicitly opts out of repo scoping (`email.WithRepoScope(func() string { return "" })`) which is directly relevant if another auditor's section touches DES-033.

Scope: Basic Types (112-125), Free Types (126-167), all \zed/\schema blocks, Key Properties (620-666). AUDIT ONLY, no edits made.

**Q1 — fuzz type-check: PASS.** `fuzz -t docs/architecture.tex`, exit 0, zero errors/warnings across all Given sets, free types, and 11 schemas. A spec that type-checks cleanly, but see below — clean typing says nothing about fidelity.

**Q2 — findings, numbered:**

1. **Trust totality/exclusivity — ACCURATE, and it's genuinely derivable, not just asserted.** Lines 190-213, 627-630. I hand-checked the case split: ZBOOL has 2 values, so the 4 boolean inputs give 16 combinations; the 4 implications in `ClassifyTrust` partition exactly on (E2E∧Internal) then (hasPGPSignature, pgpVerified), and in every branch exactly one implication's antecedent is true, forcing `level!` to one value with the other three vacuous. This is real, not decorative — worth telling whoever asked that the totality claim holds up.

2. **"No external sender is ever `trusted`" — MISSING.** `TrustInput`/`ClassifyTrust` (175-208) never models sender origin as a term; `hasProtonE2E`/`hasProtonInternal` are opaque ZBOOLs with no schema-level tie to genuine Bridge-authenticated origin. The guarantee is entirely a code-level channel-authenticity assumption (`internal/daemon/handler.go:157-160` comment: "External SMTP injection of these headers is blocked by Bridge") that the Z cannot see or check. Fix: either add an axiom relating a `SENDERORIGIN` given type to `hasProtonInternal`, or state in prose that this specific safety property is outside the schema's reach (an assumption about Bridge, not a theorem of the model).

3. **`GPGEnvironment.isolated = ztrue` (388-395) over-claims — WRONG as stated.** Verified against code: `internal/pgp/verify.go` uses an isolated GNUPGHOME; `internal/pgp/sign.go` and `internal/pgp/decrypt.go` use the default system GNUPGHOME by design (`decrypt.go:28` comment, and this same file's own Design Invariant #3, line 478-482: "Signing and decryption use the owner's own key from the system keyring"). So the schema's unconditional `isolated = ztrue` contradicts an invariant stated 90 lines later in the same document. Key Property #3 (636-638, "no PGP operation writes to the user's system keyring") repeats the over-claim. Fix: rename schema to `VerifyEnvironment` (it only ever models the verify path) and reword Property #3 to scope the isolation guarantee to verification only.

4. **Loopback-only TLS exception — WRONG/STALE, security-relevant.** Line 310-312 and Design Invariant #10 (502-504) both claim the self-signed-cert exception applies "only for loopback addresses." Actual code (`internal/email/imap.go:35`, `smtp.go:29`): `InsecureSkipVerify: cfg.TLSSkipVerify || isLoopback(...)`. A `tls_skip_verify` config field (`config.go:38`) lets an operator disable cert verification against *any* host — and `docs/TESTING.md`'s own Fastmail test config exercises exactly that non-loopback path. This claim is simply false today. Fix: "skipped for loopback addresses, or for any host when the operator explicitly sets `tls_skip_verify` — used only for out-of-band interop testing, never expected in production."

5. **"PGP Signing (Future)" subsection (372-377) — STALE, contradicted by shipped code.** Claims outbound signing is unimplemented because "Neither Proton Bridge (strips MIME) nor Resend... supports this," pending Amazon SES. But `internal/email/chain.go` (`TrySendChain`, `ComposeSignedRaw`, `ComposeEncryptedSignedRaw`) signs — and now also RFC 3156 encrypts — outbound mail over Proton Bridge SMTP today when `cfg.GPGSigner` is set. This also breaks `SendState`'s totality (346-352): `chain.go:101-103,121-122` now blocks the Resend fallback entirely when signing/encryption is configured, so `¬smtpAvailable ∧ signingRequired` yields *no* method — a case the current two-branch schema doesn't cover. Fix: replace the "Future" prose with the implemented path, and extend the schema:
   ```
   SendMethod ::= smProtonSMTP | smResend | smFailed
   ...
   smtpAvailable = zfalse ∧ signingRequired = ztrue ⟹ method! = smFailed
   ```

6. **Daemon state entirely unmodeled — scope-honesty gap, not a type error.** `internal/daemon` introduced: a pipeline `Status` field (`running`/`failed`/`completed`, `pipeline.go:30,58,204`), a `contacts.Permission{Read,Write,Execute}` rwx struct (`permissions.go:9-12`), and command-file signature verification (`signature.go:133 VerifySignature`, a *separate* trust boundary from `GPGEnvironment`/inbound-message verification). None have a schema. Worse: the doc's own Introduction (42-46) scopes itself to "`beadle-email` v0.1.x," yet §"Daemon Architecture" (546-618) and 4 of the 9 Key Properties (6-9, 648-664) describe daemon behavior in prose only — the document already violates its own stated scope, independent of Z coverage. My recommendation, per your framing: **narrow, don't expand.** Drop the Daemon Architecture section and Key Properties 6-9 into a separate `beadle-daemon` architecture doc (formalized there, since that's where the trust-and-permission-composition logic actually lives — `handler.go:148-166` also layers a contact-GPGKeyID-binding check on top of plain `verified` that `TrustLevel` alone doesn't express, so "verified" means something subtly stronger for daemon execution than for `beadle-email`'s own tools). Keep this file honestly scoped to the email channel, title already says so.

Two smaller spec-quality nits, same file, worth a line each while someone's in there:

7. `CredBackend` free type (155) is declared but never used in `CredentialStore`/`ResolveCredential` (which use three parallel `ZBOOL`-gated maps instead) — dead type, delete or actually use it.

8. `SelectFolder`'s `folder? : CREDNAME` (316) reuses the credential-name type for an IMAP folder name — type-checks fine (same carrier) but is a real category error; a distinct `FOLDERNAME` given type would catch a confusion the current typing can't.

9. `MSGID`, `HEADER`, `RAWBYTES`, `SIGNER` (declared line 116) are never used in *any* schema — the entire "Fetch and Parse" pipeline (322-340), the thing `MSGID` exists for, has zero formal backing. Either add a minimal `Message`/`FetchMessage` schema or drop the unused given types so the Basic Types section stops promising coverage it doesn't have.

Everything above I verified against current source (`internal/email/trust.go`, `internal/pgp/{verify,sign,decrypt}.go`, `internal/email/{imap,smtp,chain,config}.go`, `internal/daemon/{handler,pipeline,signature}.go`, `internal/contacts/permissions.go`) at HEAD of `docs/daemon-status-artifact`. Didn't touch anything outside my assigned sections — Package Map, MCP Tool Surface, and Security Boundaries prose are in other auditors' scope.

WHAT: when gpg_signer is configured, TrySendChain composes a multipart/signed message and sends it over whatever SMTP host email.json names. It reports success on a clean SMTP transaction. It never checks whether that host preserves raw MIME.

Proton Bridge -- the DEFAULT transport -- strips multipart/signed envelopes (DES-005). Resend/SES also strips (DES-006). So an operator who configures signing and leaves the default transport gets:

  beadle-email send ...   ->   \"sent\"
  recipient               ->   no signature, or a broken one

Nothing in the return value, the log, or the CLI output indicates the signature did not survive.

VERIFIED (internal/email/chain.go):
  :61      signing := cfg.GPGSigner != \"\"
  :89-91   composes ComposeEncryptedSignedRaw / ComposeSignedRaw
  :102     resend fallback correctly BLOCKED for signed mail
  :122     \"pgp-signed email requires SMTP transport; Resend API cannot preserve raw MIME\"
  no check anywhere that cfg.SMTPHost is a MIME-preserving host

So the Resend leg is handled well -- it refuses rather than silently downgrading, which is the right pattern. The SMTP leg has the same failure mode and no equivalent guard.

WHY IT MATTERS: the whole point of signing is that the recipient can verify. A signature stripped in transit is indistinguishable, from the sender's side, from one that arrived intact. The system already knows which transports strip -- it is recorded in DESIGN.md DES-005/DES-006 and in docs/TESTING.md, which documents switching to Fastmail SMTP (port 465, implicit TLS) specifically because it preserves the envelope (verified 2026-04-11).

This is the same class as the guards fixed in beadle-5k5 and beadle-k1g: a path that abandons its purpose and reports success.

SCOPE OF FIX -- needs a decision, do not assume:
  1. Warn at send time when signing is configured and SMTPHost is a known-stripping host (127.0.0.1 Proton Bridge, Resend). Cheapest, keeps the send working.
  2. Refuse outright, mirroring the Resend leg's behavior at chain.go:122. Most consistent, but breaks any operator relying on best-effort signed sends today.
  3. Return a structured result flagging signature-preservation as unverified, letting the caller decide.
Recommend 1 now and consider 2 once beadle-7gm's onboarding exists to guide transport choice. Do NOT hardcode a Fastmail allowlist -- that ages badly; key off the known-stripping set, which is what we actually have evidence for.

TEST: send signed over a stripping host, assert the warning or refusal. A negative case must confirm a preserving host does not trigger it.

DOC: architecture.tex's send-path true-up states this explicitly -- that TrySendChain does not validate the transport for MIME preservation and will report 'sent' for a signature broken on the wire." 2>&1 | tail -2

\subsection{External Origin: An Assumption, Not a Theorem}

\textit{ClassifyTrust} proves that every combination of its four
$ZBOOL$ inputs is mapped to exactly one $TrustLevel$ (a routine case
split on $hasProtonE2E$, $hasProtonInternal$, $hasPGPSignature$, and
$pgpVerified$, each of which has only two values).  It does \emph{not}
prove the stronger property this repository actually depends on: that
no externally-originated message is ever classified $trusted$.  It
cannot, because nothing in $TrustInput$ says where a message came
from --- $hasProtonE2E$ and $hasProtonInternal$ are bare booleans, and
the schema has no way to ask whether they are telling the truth.

\begin{zed}
  Origin ::= originInternal | originExternal
\end{zed}

\begin{schema}{ChannelAssumption}
  origin : Origin \\
  hasProtonE2E : ZBOOL \\
  hasProtonInternal : ZBOOL
  \where
  origin = originExternal \implies
    \lnot (hasProtonE2E = ztrue \land hasProtonInternal = ztrue)
\end{schema}

$origin$ is ground truth: where the message actually came from, not
what its headers claim.  \textit{ChannelAssumption} is not derived
from anything else in this document --- it is posited, and its truth
depends entirely on Proton Bridge behaving as documented (setting
\texttt{X-Pm-Content-Encryption}/\texttt{X-Pm-Origin} only for
messages it has itself routed end-to-end between two Proton
mailboxes, and stripping or refusing to forward those headers on
anything externally injected).  \texttt{internal/daemon/handler.go}
records the same assumption in a code comment rather than an
enforced check: \textit{``External SMTP injection of these headers is
blocked by Bridge''} --- exactly the kind of claim a Z schema cannot
verify and should not pretend to.

Given \textit{ChannelAssumption}, the property this repository relies
on follows as a theorem, not as decoration: by \textit{ClassifyTrust},
$hasProtonE2E = ztrue \land hasProtonInternal = ztrue$ is the only
condition that entails $level! = trusted$, and by the totality proved
above no other input combination also entails it; by
\textit{ChannelAssumption}'s contrapositive, that same condition
entails $origin = originInternal$.  So $level! = trusted \implies
origin = originInternal$ --- \emph{no external sender is ever
trusted} --- but only for as long as \textit{ChannelAssumption} holds.
If Bridge is ever misconfigured, or a future defect lets an external
SMTP client set these two headers, this specification gives no
warning: the assumption, not a theorem about message content, is
where that guarantee actually lives.

\subsection{PGP Signing and Encryption}

Outbound PGP signing is implemented, not future work: when
\texttt{cfg.GPGSigner} is configured, every message sent over Proton

\section{Introduction}
%%----------------------------------------------------------------------

Beadle is an autonomous agent daemon with cryptographic owner control.
Command \emph{execution} requires a GPG-signed command file authorized
by the owner (\S~Command-File Signature Verification); the daemon has
no independent decision-making about \emph{what to run}. The earlier
steps that decide whether to create a pipeline at all --- sender
permission and transport-trust checks --- carry no such signature (\S~Daemon
Architecture, Design Invariant~1). ``Owner'' here names the single GPG
key \texttt{daemon.json} designates as the recipe authorizer (via
\texttt{owner\_handle} or \texttt{owner\_gpg\_key\_id}), not a general
position of authority over the system; a rename to ``authorizer'' is
proposed under bead beadle-4ul but not yet done.

\texttt{beadle-email} shipped first: an MCP server and CLI that provide
email communication via Proton Bridge with a four-level PGP trust
model. \texttt{beadle-daemon} is a second binary, sharing
\texttt{beadle-email}'s lower package layers, that acts on that mail
unattended (\S~System Overview, \S~Daemon Architecture). This document
describes both binaries: their package structure, data flows, security
boundaries, and key state machines formalised in Z.

%%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{System Overview}
%%----------------------------------------------------------------------

Beadle ships as two independent binaries sharing package layers.
\texttt{beadle-email} exposes an MCP server and CLI for message
send/receive/triage; \texttt{beadle-daemon} watches a mailbox
unattended and turns authorized instructions into mission pipelines.
Neither imports the other at the command layer (\S~Dependency Graph).

\subsection{beadle-email}

\texttt{beadle-email} runs as an MCP server, by default over stdio;
\texttt{serve --transport ws} instead starts a WebSocket listener
(\S~Security Boundaries).  It connects to Proton Bridge via IMAP on
localhost by default --- a config default, not an enforced boundary
(\S~Security Boundaries) --- sends mail via Proton Bridge SMTP
(primary) or Resend API (fallback), and verifies PGP signatures using
an isolated GPG keyring.

The binary groups its subcommands by concern: server administration
(\texttt{serve}, \texttt{doctor}, \texttt{status}, \texttt{version},
\texttt{health}), message operations (\texttt{list}, \texttt{search},
\texttt{read}, \texttt{send}, \texttt{reply}, \texttt{move},
\texttt{mark}, \texttt{folders}), contact management
(\texttt{contact list|add|remove|find}), identity
(\texttt{identity show|set}), and enablement (\texttt{enable}/
\texttt{disable}, \texttt{install}/\texttt{uninstall}).  Run
\texttt{beadle-email --help} for the current, authoritative list ---
it changes independently of this document.

\subsection{beadle-daemon}

\texttt{beadle-daemon} has no MCP surface at all --- it does not
import \texttt{internal/mcp} (\S~Dependency Graph).  Its single
subcommand, \texttt{run}, polls the mailbox, checks sender permission
and transport trust (\S~Daemon Architecture), and on a pass executes a
signed-command pipeline.  It is implemented but not released:
\texttt{make build-daemon} builds it locally, but no CI workflow and
no \texttt{make dist} target produces a distributable binary (bead
beadle-5ma).

\subsection{Proton Bridge SMTP}

SMTP uses implicit TLS on port 465, or STARTTLS otherwise, with the
same self-signed certificate exception as IMAP for loopback addresses
--- extended to any host when \texttt{tls\_skip\_verify} is set
(Design Invariant~10).  Port 465 implicit TLS is also the branch the
Fastmail signing transport uses (\S~PGP Signing).  Authentication uses
\texttt{PLAIN} with \texttt{smtp-password} if configured, else the
same credentials as IMAP (\S~Credential Resolution).  The raw RFC~822
message is composed by \texttt{ComposeRaw}, which validates header
fields against CR/LF injection.

\subsection{Resend API}

The Resend fallback sends via HTTPS POST to
\texttt{api.resend.com/emails}.  It supports both plain text and
HTML bodies.  The API key is resolved via the credential store.

\subsection{PGP Signing}

PGP signing of outbound mail (DES-022, SETTLED) requires a transport
that preserves raw MIME (\texttt{multipart/signed} envelopes).
Neither Proton Bridge (strips MIME) nor Resend (no raw MIME API;
Resend's own backend is Amazon SES, which strips it the same way)
supports this.  The signing transport that does is \textbf{Fastmail
SMTP} on port 465 (implicit TLS, \S~Proton Bridge SMTP) --- selected
by pointing \texttt{smtp\_host}/\texttt{smtp\_port} at Fastmail (see
\texttt{docs/TESTING.md}'s Fastmail Test Config).

\texttt{TrySendChain} does not itself validate that the transport it
used preserved the signed MIME envelope --- it reports success on any
clean SMTP transaction.  A signed message sent over the default
(Proton Bridge) configuration reports ``sent'' while carrying a
signature Bridge has already stripped; only a transport actually known
to preserve \texttt{multipart/signed}, such as Fastmail, makes the
signature meaningful on arrival.

\subsection{Sign Flow}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Check the signer key's expiry (\texttt{checkSignerKeyExpiry})
    before any other work --- keys with no expiration date, or an
    expiration date already passed, are rejected before boundary
    generation or body composition even begins.
  \item Compose the body as a MIME part with CRLF line endings
    (mandatory per RFC~3156).
  \item Write the GPG passphrase to a temporary file (mode 600) to
    avoid exposing it in process arguments or \texttt{ps} output.
  \item Run \texttt{gpg --detach-sign --armor} with
    \texttt{--passphrase-file}.
  \item Assemble the full RFC~822 message with a
    \texttt{multipart/signed} envelope containing the body part and
    detached signature.
  \item Generate the MIME boundary using \texttt{crypto/rand}.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Command-File Signature Verification}

Command-file verification (\texttt{internal/daemon/signature.go}'s
\texttt{VerifySignature}, DES-034/DES-035, both SETTLED) is a
structurally distinct, stricter path from \texttt{pgp.Verify} above:
it authorizes a \emph{command definition}, not an inbound message.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Reconstruct the canonical bytes that were signed --- the
    command with its \texttt{Signature} field cleared, marshaled
    deterministically (\texttt{CanonicalCommandBytes}).
  \item Create an isolated GNUPGHOME, as with inbound verification.
  \item Import \emph{only} the authorizer's key (identified by a full
    40-hex fingerprint\footnote{\texttt{daemon.json}'s
    \texttt{owner\_handle}/\texttt{owner\_gpg\_key\_id} name this key
    as ``owner'' in code and config today; a rename to
    ``authorizer'' is proposed under bead beadle-4ul but not yet
    done.  This document uses ``authorizer'' for the concept and the
    current field names for the literal config keys.}) from the
    ambient keyring into the isolated one, and assert exactly one key
    with that exact fingerprint landed there --- never a silent
    ``verify against whatever's there.''
  \item Check that key's expiry against the isolated homedir (Design
    Invariant~4).
  \item Run \texttt{gpg --verify --status-fd} and parse the
    machine-readable \texttt{[GNUPG:]} status lines: every outcome
    except \texttt{GOODSIG} is an error, classified by reason
    (missing, invalid, wrong-key, key-expired).  This is a stricter
    parse than \texttt{pgp.Verify}'s, which reads a stderr substring.
\end{enumerate}

A nil error means the authorizer, and only the authorizer, signed this
exact command definition with a key that has not expired.
\texttt{LoadCommands}/\texttt{loadCommand} call \texttt{VerifySignature}
on every command file at daemon startup; when \texttt{daemon.json} is
absent, unresolvable, or names both or neither owner field, command
loading is disabled entirely --- the daemon starts with zero commands
rather than falling back to unsigned execution.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Zero agent authority (command execution only).}
    Every command the daemon executes requires a GPG-signed command
    file authorized by the owner (\S~Command-File Signature
    Verification) --- the daemon has no independent decision-making
    about \emph{what to run}.  This does not cover every action taken
    on inbound mail: \texttt{OnNewMail} creates a pipeline or a bare
    mission record from sender permission and transport trust alone,
    with no signed command anywhere in that earlier decision
    (\S~Daemon Architecture, Detection and Trust Gate).  With zero
    commands loaded, nothing downstream runs, but the mission/pipeline
    record itself is still created.

  \item \textbf{Preflight before execute.}  All permissions are
    validated before any command runs.  No partial execution.

  \item \textbf{Isolated verification.}  Inbound signature verification
    runs in a temporary GNUPGHOME so an untrusted sender's key never
    touches the system keyring. Signing and decryption use the owner's
    own key from the system keyring, since that is where it already
    lives.

  \item \textbf{Expired and non-expiring keys rejected.}  All
    command-signing keys must carry an expiration date that has not
    yet passed --- enforced on the primary key and, when the key has
    signing-capable subkeys, requiring at least one such subkey with a
    current, non-expired expiry (\texttt{internal/pgp/expiry.go}).

  \item \textbf{Audit log is tamperproof (designed, not
    implemented).}  Append-only, GPG-signed entries; only the owner
    can clear the log.  No code implements this today ---
    \texttt{internal/daemon} has no audit-log type, writer, or clear
    operation (bead beadle-623).  This invariant is retained as the
    design target, not a description of current behavior.

```latex
%%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Daemon Formalisation}
%%----------------------------------------------------------------------

The sections above cover \texttt{beadle-email} v0.1.x.
\texttt{beadle-daemon} is a second binary with its own state and its
own trust boundary; this section formalises the three pieces of
daemon-only state a defect audit found completely unmodeled:
pipeline lifecycle, per-contact permission, and command-file
signature verification --- plus the gate that composes all three,
together with the email channel's own trust model, into one
admission decision.  Nothing here models pipeline \emph{file}
lifecycle (retention, archival, deletion): that mechanism is
designed (DES-032) but not implemented ---
\texttt{internal/daemon/command.go} has no file-flow fields --- and a
schema for it here would misrepresent designed-only behaviour as
shipped.

\begin{zed}
  [CMDID]
\end{zed}

$CMDID$ identifies one command file by its declared name (the map
key in \texttt{internal/daemon.Command}'s registry), not by its
file path or its content hash.

\subsection{Pipeline Lifecycle}

\begin{zed}
  PipelineStatus ::= psRunning | psFailed | psCompleted
\end{zed}

Three states, matching \texttt{internal/daemon/pipeline.go}'s
\texttt{Status} field exactly: $psRunning$ while a pipeline's stages
are still executing, $psFailed$ on any stage error or on daemon
restart with the pipeline still in flight (Crash Recovery, Key
Property~9 below), $psCompleted$ once every stage --- including the
auto-appended reply --- has finished.  A completed pipeline may
still carry a non-fatal auto-reply error (\texttt{Pipeline.Error});
\textit{PipelineStatus} says nothing about that field, by design ---
test $status$ for success, not $Error$, exactly as the Go comment on
\texttt{Pipeline.Error} instructs.

\begin{schema}{Pipeline}
  status : PipelineStatus
\end{schema}

\begin{schema}{PipelineTransition}
  \Delta Pipeline
  \where
  (status \neq psRunning \implies status' = status) \\
  \land \\
  (status' = psRunning \implies status = psRunning)
\end{schema}

\textit{PipelineTransition} states the property this section exists
to capture: a pipeline that leaves $psRunning$ never returns to it,
and in fact never changes state again at all --- $psFailed$ and
$psCompleted$ are absorbing.  The first conjunct pins a
non-running pipeline's status; the second forbids any transition
\emph{into} $psRunning$ except from $psRunning$ itself.  Together
they leave exactly one live transition family: $psRunning \to
psRunning$, $psRunning \to psFailed$, and $psRunning \to
psCompleted$ are all permitted; nothing else is.

\subsection{Per-Contact Permission}

\begin{schema}{Permission}
  read : ZBOOL \\
  write : ZBOOL \\
  execute : ZBOOL
\end{schema}

The three bits are independent --- \textit{Permission} carries no
$\where$ clause because nothing in \texttt{internal/contacts}
couples them.  A contact can hold $execute = ztrue \land read =
zfalse$ (execute-only) exactly as validly as any other combination;
this schema does not narrow that.

\subsection{Command-File Signature Verification}

\begin{zed}
  CommandSigOutcome ::= csGood | csMissing | csWrongKey
                       | csExpired | csInvalid
\end{zed}

The five outcomes correspond exactly to
\texttt{internal/daemon/signature.go}'s \texttt{SignatureReason}
constants ($csMissing$, $csInvalid$, $csWrongKey$, $csExpired$) plus
$csGood$, its unstated fifth case: a $nil$ \texttt{error} from
\texttt{VerifySignature}.  $csInvalid$ covers everything the Go
comment calls \emph{``do not trust this signature''} ---
\texttt{BADSIG}, \texttt{ERRSIG}, \texttt{REVKEYSIG},
\texttt{EXPSIG}, a malformed owner fingerprint, and any unrecognised
\texttt{gpg --status-fd} line, none of which get their own outcome
because none of them get their own \texttt{SignatureReason} in the
Go code either.

\begin{schema}{CommandSigInput}
  fingerprintValid : ZBOOL \\
  hasSignature : ZBOOL \\
  importedKeyCount : \nat \\
  keyExpired : ZBOOL \\
  sawGoodSig : ZBOOL \\
  sawExpKeySig : ZBOOL \\
  sawNoPubkey : ZBOOL \\
  sawBadOrErrSig : ZBOOL
\end{schema}

$fingerprintValid$ is whether the configured owner key ID matches a
40-hex OpenPGP fingerprint.  $importedKeyCount$ is the number of
keys with exactly that fingerprint found in the isolated keyring
after import --- this is what makes command-file verification
\emph{stricter} than inbound message verification:
\textit{VerifyEnvironment} (above) imports every system key, or
whatever key the message itself attached, with no uniqueness
requirement; \textit{CommandSigInput} imports \emph{one named key}
and treats anything other than exactly one match as a hard failure,
never a ``pick one.''  The four $saw$-prefixed fields mirror
\texttt{classifyStatusLines}'s four collected \texttt{[GNUPG:]}
status lines; $sawBadOrErrSig$ covers
\texttt{BADSIG}/\texttt{ERRSIG}/\texttt{REVKEYSIG}/\texttt{EXPSIG}
together, since all four collapse to the same $csInvalid$ outcome
below.

\begin{schema}{VerifyCommandSignature}
  CommandSigInput \\
  outcome! : CommandSigOutcome
  \where
  (fingerprintValid = zfalse \implies outcome! = csInvalid) \\
  \land \\
  (fingerprintValid = ztrue \land hasSignature = zfalse
    \implies outcome! = csMissing) \\
  \land \\
  (fingerprintValid = ztrue \land hasSignature = ztrue
    \land importedKeyCount \neq 1
    \implies outcome! = csInvalid) \\
  \land \\
  (fingerprintValid = ztrue \land hasSignature = ztrue
    \land importedKeyCount = 1 \land keyExpired = ztrue
    \implies outcome! = csExpired) \\
  \land \\
  (fingerprintValid = ztrue \land hasSignature = ztrue
    \land importedKeyCount = 1 \land keyExpired = zfalse
    \land sawNoPubkey = ztrue
    \implies outcome! = csWrongKey) \\
  \land \\
  (fingerprintValid = ztrue \land hasSignature = ztrue
    \land importedKeyCount = 1 \land keyExpired = zfalse
    \land sawNoPubkey = zfalse \land sawGoodSig = ztrue
    \implies outcome! = csGood) \\
  \land \\
  (fingerprintValid = ztrue \land hasSignature = ztrue
    \land importedKeyCount = 1 \land keyExpired = zfalse
    \land sawNoPubkey = zfalse \land sawGoodSig = zfalse
    \land sawExpKeySig = ztrue
    \implies outcome! = csExpired) \\
  \land \\
  (fingerprintValid = ztrue \land hasSignature = ztrue
    \land importedKeyCount = 1 \land keyExpired = zfalse
    \land sawNoPubkey = zfalse \land sawGoodSig = zfalse
    \land sawExpKeySig = zfalse
    \implies outcome! = csInvalid)
\end{schema}

The eight cases are exhaustive and mutually exclusive by the same
construction as \textit{ClassifyTrust}: each guard rules out every
earlier one, so exactly one implication's antecedent holds for any
assignment to the eight inputs, and $outcome!$ is forced accordingly.
Only one branch reaches $csGood$ --- everything else, including an
unrecognised status line that matches none of the four $saw$ flags,
is an error.  That is \texttt{classifyStatusLines}'s own invariant,
stated in its comment as ``there is no implicit fallthrough to
nil''; this schema is that invariant, checked.

The canonical payload that gets signed is \texttt{cmd} with its
\texttt{Signature} field cleared to the empty string
(\texttt{CanonicalCommandBytes}) --- not modeled as a separate
schema here, in keeping with this document's practice of leaving
byte-level serialisation to prose (the same choice already made for
\texttt{ComposeRaw} and \texttt{ParseMIME}).  The property that
matters formally is that signing and verifying agree on what
``canonical'' means because both call the same function; nothing in
\textit{CommandSigInput} depends on \texttt{Signature}'s own bytes.

\begin{schema}{LoadedCommands}
  commands : \power CMDID \\
  sigOutcome : CMDID \pfun CommandSigOutcome
  \where
  commands = \{ c : \dom sigOutcome | sigOutcome(c) = csGood \}
\end{schema}

Command-file signature verification does not happen per email: it
happens once, when \texttt{LoadCommands} reads the command directory
at daemon startup (\texttt{internal/daemon/command.go}).  A command
that fails verification is simply absent from $commands$ --- it can
never be selected by the planner for any message, however trusted.
\textit{LoadedCommands} is the daemon's runnable command set; it
does not vary per inbound message the way \textit{DaemonGate} below
does.

\subsection{The Execution Gate}

\begin{schema}{DaemonGate}
  Permission \\
  LoadedCommands \\
  trust : TrustLevel \\
  keyBound : ZBOOL \\
  cmd? : CMDID \\
  admit! : ZBOOL
  \where
  admit! = ztrue \iff
    ((trust = trusted) \lor (trust = verified \land keyBound = ztrue))
    \land execute = ztrue \land cmd? \in commands
\end{schema}

\textit{DaemonGate} is where the trust model (\S~``Trust Model''),
per-contact permission, and command-file signature verification
meet.  Execution requires all three, independently: transport trust
at $trusted$ or $verified$ \emph{and} the sender's $execute$ bit
\emph{and} a command that survived \textit{VerifyCommandSignature}
at load time.

$keyBound$ makes explicit an asymmetry the code has but the trust
model above does not state: for daemon execution, $verified$ is not
enough on its own.  \texttt{internal/daemon/handler.go}'s
\texttt{verifyTrust} additionally requires that, when a contact has
a registered \texttt{GPGKeyID}, the signing key on the message
actually matches it --- a mismatch is treated as $untrusted$, not as
``verified but unbound.''  $keyBound$ is $ztrue$ exactly when the
contact has no registered key, or the signer's key matches the one
it has.  The Go implementation folds this directly into the
\texttt{TrustLevel} it returns (a key mismatch computes as
$untrusted$ before \textit{DaemonGate} ever sees it); this schema
pulls the two conditions apart because that is what makes the
asymmetry with \texttt{beadle-email}'s own, unbound notion of
$verified$ visible at all.  Read literally, \textit{DaemonGate}'s
$trust = verified \land keyBound = ztrue$ disjunct is therefore
never the operative check in the running system ---
\texttt{verifyTrust} has already collapsed it into $trust$ itself by
the time this schema's predicate runs --- but the two formulations
denote the same function, and only the decomposed one documents why
``verified'' means something stronger here than it does for
\texttt{beadle-email}'s own tools.
```

\section{Daemon Architecture}
%%----------------------------------------------------------------------

\texttt{beadle-daemon} is a standalone Go process that monitors email
autonomously and executes multi-stage pipelines when authorised
contacts send instructions.

\subsection{Detection and Trust Gate}

The daemon reuses the same \texttt{Poller} as \texttt{beadle-email},
decoupled via a \texttt{NewMailFunc} callback.  When new mail is
detected, the handler (\texttt{OnNewMail}, DES-027, SETTLED):

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Fetches recent unread messages via IMAP.
  \item Looks up the sender in the contact store.
  \item Checks the \texttt{x} (execute) permission bit.
  \item Verifies transport trust --- Proton E2E (trusted) or PGP
    signature with key bound to contact (verified).  Unverified
    messages from \texttt{rwx} contacts are rejected.  Trust in the
    Proton-E2E branch rests on IMAP actually being Proton Bridge on
    localhost, which nothing here confirms yet (bead beadle-hv7i).
  \item On pass: creates a pipeline when a spawner and command
    templates are configured; otherwise falls back to a bare mission
    record (\texttt{h.missions.Create}) with no pipeline or signed
    command involved at all (Design Invariant~1).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Pipeline Orchestrator}

A pipeline decomposes an email instruction into a sequence of typed
commands (DES-030, DES-031, both SETTLED).  Each command is a
GPG-signed YAML definition (\S~Command-File Signature Verification)
with a typed argument schema, write-set, budget, timeout, and tool
list, run by one of two runners:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{claude} --- spawns an ephemeral \texttt{claude -p
    --bare} session per stage (\S~Worker Isolation).
  \item \textbf{cli} --- runs a whitelisted binary directly, or a
    compound sequence of binaries declared as \texttt{steps}, chained
    together via \texttt{io.Pipe} goroutines.  A binary's resolved,
    symlink-followed path (\texttt{filepath.EvalSymlinks}) must still
    land inside a whitelisted directory.  Output is capped at 1~MB
    (\texttt{io.LimitReader}); anything beyond the cap is discarded
    and the result is marked truncated, not silently grown.
\end{itemize}

A stage's data flows to the next through a top-level \texttt{pipe}
value, shaped by each command's declared \texttt{mode}:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \texttt{process} --- the stage's output replaces \texttt{pipe}
    for the next stage, after validation against the command's
    \texttt{output\_schema} (\texttt{"text"} or a JSON Schema object).
  \item \texttt{passthrough} --- \texttt{pipe} is unchanged; the
    stage's own result is still recorded like any other stage.
\end{itemize}

Stage args and the prior stage's pipeline output are carried to the
worker as free text in the mission contract's top-level
\texttt{context} field --- ethos's \texttt{inputs} schema recognizes
only \texttt{trigger}, \texttt{files}, \texttt{ticket}, and
\texttt{references}; there is no \texttt{inputs.args} or
\texttt{inputs.previous\_output} field under any name.  Assuming
otherwise is exactly what shipped broken as beadle-8gt.

\begin{verbatim}
  Email instruction
    -> Planner (LLM or rule-based)
    -> [cmd1 (process/passthrough) | cmd2 | ... | auto-reply]
    -> Sequential mission execution; context field carries stage
       args + prior pipe value
\end{verbatim}

File-flow support --- attachments and generated artifacts moving
between stages as file references, rather than only through
\texttt{pipe} --- is designed (DES-032) but not implemented:
\texttt{Command} has no file-flow fields today.

\subsection{Worker Isolation}

Isolation here is process-level only, not container-level: workers
share the daemon host's kernel, network namespace, and filesystem
outside their restricted \texttt{PATH}.  Container isolation (network
namespace, seccomp) is an unfiled TODO in \texttt{spawner.go}, not yet
implemented.  Within that scope, workers run with:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \texttt{--bare} mode (no hooks, plugins, CLAUDE.md).
  \item Restricted PATH: the resolved \texttt{claude} binary's own
    directory, plus \texttt{/usr/bin} and \texttt{/usr/local/bin}.
  \item Per-command MCP servers from a registry.
  \item Adversarial robustness instructions in the system prompt.
  \item 30-minute timeout, \$5 budget cap, 50-turn limit --- each
    overridable; these are the defaults.
  \item Protected env vars (HOME, PATH, ANTHROPIC\_API\_KEY) forced
    after command overrides.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Pipeline Persistence}

Pipeline state is written to
\texttt{\~{}/.punt-labs/beadle/pipelines/<id>.json} via atomic rename
(write to \texttt{.tmp-<id>.json}, then \texttt{os.Rename}) at each
state transition, under 0700/0600 permissions, with a path-traversal
guard on the pipeline ID.  On daemon startup, in-flight
(\texttt{"running"}) pipelines are marked failed and the originator is
notified.  A 30-day retention sweep runs on a recurring ticker
(\texttt{DefaultRetention}); orphaned \texttt{.tmp-*.json} files left
by a process that died between write and rename are reaped separately,
after 5 minutes, since a torn write may not even parse as a pipeline
record.  \texttt{cmd/beadle-daemon}'s \texttt{main} wires this store
into both the startup sweep and the \texttt{Executor} that runs live
pipelines, so both see the same records.
